claim: The hemispheric, bi-layered optic cup forms from an oval optic vesicle during early vertebrate eye development through major morphological transformations.
source: The hemispheric, bi-layered optic cup forms from an oval optic vesicle during early vertebrate eye development through major morphological transformations.
evidence: This is a general statement about vertebrate eye development that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: During optic cup formation, the overall basal surface facing the developing lens is increasing.
source: The overall basal surface, facing the developing lens, is increasing, while, at the same time, the space basally occupied by individual cells is decreasing.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements and observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: During optic cup formation, the space basally occupied by individual cells is decreasing.
source: The overall basal surface, facing the developing lens, is increasing, while, at the same time, the space basally occupied by individual cells is decreasing.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of basal constriction in retinal progenitor cells.

claim: The classical view of eye development cannot explain the simultaneous increase in basal surface area and decrease in space occupied by individual cells.
source: This cannot be explained by the classical view of eye development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incompatibility between observed data and existing models.

claim: The lens-averted epithelium functions as a reservoir that contributes to the growing neuroretina through epithelial flow around the distal rims of the optic cup.
source: Using zebrafish (Danio rerio) as a model, we show that the lens-averted epithelium functions as a reservoir that contributes to the growing neuroretina through epithelial flow around the distal rims of the optic cup.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4D imaging data showing cell movements during optic cup formation.

claim: Epithelial flow couples morphogenesis and retinal determination.
source: We propose that this flow couples morphogenesis and retinal determination.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the observed relationship between cell movement and differentiation.

claim: Future stem cells flow from their origin in the lens-averted domain of the optic vesicle to their destination in the ciliary marginal zone.
source: Our 4D data indicate that future stem cells flow from their origin in the lens-averted domain of the optic vesicle to their destination in the ciliary marginal zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell tracking data from 4D imaging experiments.

claim: BMP-mediated inhibition of epithelial flow results in ectopic neuroretina in the RPE domain.
source: BMP-mediated inhibition of the flow results in ectopic neuroretina in the RPE domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental manipulation of BMP signaling and observation of resulting phenotypes.

claim: BMP-mediated inhibition of epithelial flow results in failure of the ventral fissure to close, resulting in coloboma.
source: Ultimately the ventral fissure fails to close resulting in coloboma.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of optic fissure closure defects in BMP-treated embryos.

claim: The bi-layered optic vesicles of vertebrates are formed through a bilateral evagination of the late prosencephalon.
source: The bi-layered optic vesicles of vertebrates are formed through a bilateral evagination of the late prosencephalon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate eye development.

claim: In teleosts, optic vesicle formation is driven by a migration of single cells that undergo a subsequent intercalation into the epithelium of the expanding optic vesicle.
source: In teleosts, this process is driven by a migration of single cells that undergo a subsequent intercalation into the epithelium of the expanding optic vesicle (Rembold et al., 2006, England et al., 2006, Sinn and Wittbrodt, 2013, Ivanovitch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on teleost eye development.

claim: The classical view proposes that the lens-averted epithelium of the optic vesicle differentiates into the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE).
source: A long-held view of this process proposes that the lens-averted epithelium of the optic vesicle differentiates into the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE), while the epithelium facing the lens gives rise to the neuroretina, which subsequently bends around the developing lens (Chow and Lang, 2001; Fuhrmann, 2010; Walls, 1942).
evidence: This claim describes the classical model and is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The classical view proposes that the epithelium facing the lens gives rise to the neuroretina, which subsequently bends around the developing lens.
source: A long-held view of this process proposes that the lens-averted epithelium of the optic vesicle differentiates into the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE), while the epithelium facing the lens gives rise to the neuroretina, which subsequently bends around the developing lens (Chow and Lang, 2001; Fuhrmann, 2010; Walls, 1942).
evidence: This claim describes the classical model and is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neuroepithelial bending is driven by a basal constriction of lens-facing retinal progenitor cells (RPC).
source: This neuroepithelial bending is driven by a basal constriction of lens-facing retinal progenitor cells (RPC) (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009) (Bogdanović et al., 2012), which ultimately reduces the space occupied by an individual RPC at the basal surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the cellular mechanisms of optic cup formation.

claim: Basal constriction of retinal progenitor cells reduces the space occupied by an individual RPC at the basal surface.
source: This neuroepithelial bending is driven by a basal constriction of lens-facing retinal progenitor cells (RPC) (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009) (Bogdanović et al., 2012), which ultimately reduces the space occupied by an individual RPC at the basal surface.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of basal constriction and is supported by cited research.

claim: The basal optic cup surface area increases 4.7-fold from early to late optic cup stage.
source: However, we observed that this is accompanied by a 4.7-fold increase in the overall basal optic cup surface area (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Almost the entire bi-layered optic vesicle gives rise to the neural retina, with the marked exception of a small lens-averted patch.
source: Strikingly, and in contrast to the former model (Chow and Lang, 2001; Fuhrmann, 2010; Walls, 1942), our analysis shows that almost the entire bi-layered optic vesicle gives rise to the neural retina (Figure 1D–I), with the marked exception of a small lens-averted patch (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: The majority of the lens-averted epithelium serves as a neuro-epithelial reservoir that is fully integrated into the lens-facing neuro-epithelium.
source: The majority of the lens-averted epithelium (Figure 1D,G, between arrowheads) serves as a neuro-epithelial reservoir, which eventually is fully integrated into the lens-facing neuro-epithelium (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Integration of the lens-averted epithelium into the optic cup occurs through a sheet-like flow of lens-averted cells into the forming optic cup.
source: This occurs through a sheet-like flow of lens-averted cells into the forming optic cup (Figure 1E,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Epithelial flow is independent of cell proliferation.
source: This epithelial flow is independent of cell proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 2) as demonstrated by aphidicolin treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using aphidicolin to inhibit cell proliferation.

claim: The epithelial flow process is highly reminiscent of gastrulation movements.
source: The process is highly reminiscent of gastrulation movements and explains the marked increase of the lens-facing basal neuroretinal surface area.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on similarities to known developmental processes.

claim: A small domain of the lens-averted epithelium exhibits a different morphology and behavior from the rest of the lens-averted epithelium.
source: Notably, a small domain of the lens-averted epithelium exhibits a different morphology and behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging.

claim: As optic cup formation proceeds, a small region of the lens-averted epithelium flattens, enlarges, and exhibits the morphological characteristics of RPE.
source: As optic cup formation proceeds, this region flattens, enlarges, exhibits the morphological characteristics of RPE, and eventually ceases expressing RX2, a marker for retinal stem and early progenitor cells (Figure 1H, asterisks, Video 3, in between arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging and marker expression.

claim: The small RPE-forming region eventually ceases expressing RX2, a marker for retinal stem and early progenitor cells.
source: As optic cup formation proceeds, this region flattens, enlarges, exhibits the morphological characteristics of RPE, and eventually ceases expressing RX2, a marker for retinal stem and early progenitor cells (Figure 1H, asterisks, Video 3, in between arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of RX2 expression patterns over time.

claim: There is a prominent epithelial flow around the temporal perimeter of the forming optic cup concomitant with lens formation.
source: We found, concomitant with lens formation, a prominent epithelial flow around the temporal perimeter of the forming optic cup.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4D imaging data.

claim: An involution of cells from the domain of the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) into the domain of the neuroretina had been proposed.
source: An involution of cells from the domain of the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) into the domain of the neuroretina had been proposed (Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim references a previous hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Reorganization of the lens-averted and the lens-facing epithelia affecting the temporal optic cup has been described.
source: Such reorganization of the lens-averted and the lens-facing epithelia, affecting the temporal optic cup, has been subsequently described (Picker et al., 2009) and confirmed (Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It was proposed that 'rim movements' could occur around most of the optic vesicle circumference.
source: It was proposed that such 'rim movements' could occur around most of the optic vesicle circumference (Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim references a previous hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Epithelial flow occurs around the nasal perimeter into the forming optic cup.
source: Our data confirm a flow around the temporal perimeter and additionally demonstrate epithelial flow around the nasal perimeter into the forming optic cup.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4D imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The direction of the epithelial flow primarily establishes two distinct neuroretinal domains (nasal and temporal) separated by the static dorsal and ventral poles of the forming eye.
source: We uncover that the direction of the epithelial flow primarily establishes two distinct neuroretinal domains (nasal and temporal) separated by the static dorsal and ventral poles of the forming eye (Figure 2D, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cell movement patterns from imaging data.

claim: The prominent rotation of the eye cup only occurs after the epithelial flow has ceased (24–36 hpf).
source: Importantly, the prominent rotation of the eye cup only occurs after the epithelial flow has ceased (24–36 hpf, Schmitt and Dowling, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal observations and a citation to previous research.

claim: The prospective RPE remains in the lens-averted domain and expands in conjunction with the bi-furcated flow of the neuroretina from the lens-averted into the lens-facing domain.
source: The prospective RPE remains in the lens-averted domain and expands in conjunction with the bi-furcated flow of the neuroretina from the lens-averted into the lens-facing domain (Figure 2A,B, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging.

claim: The most prominent movements leading to the extension in the dorsal ventral axis occurred in the ventral domain.
source: We found that the most prominent movements leading to the extension in the dorsal ventral axis occurred in the ventral domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of cellular movements.

claim: A key step in the formation of the ventral neuroretina is the formation of the optic fissure at the ventral pole of the optic vesicle.
source: A key step in the formation of the ventral neuroretina is the formation of the optic fissure at the ventral pole of the optic vesicle.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about a developmental process observed in the study.

claim: Lens-averted epithelium flows through the optic fissure into the forming optic cup to constitute the ventral neuroepithelium.
source: Lens-averted epithelium flows through this fissure into the forming optic cup to constitute the ventral neuroepithelium (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from imaging data.

claim: The distal retinal domain (the future CMZ) originates from two distinct domains (nasal and temporal) within the lens-averted epithelium at the optic vesicle stage.
source: By tracking individual cells, we identified the origin of the distal retinal domain, the future CMZ, as two distinct domains (nasal and temporal) within the lens-averted epithelium at the optic vesicle stage (Figure 3A,B, Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell tracking data from 4D imaging.

claim: Cells show high motility in an early phase but directed flow is established only in a later phase.
source: Although cells show high motility in an early phase (Figure 3D, 1), the directed flow is established only in a later phase (Figure 3D, 2), in which cells ultimately flow to the rim of the forming optic cup (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cell tracking data showing distinct phases of movement.

claim: The dorsal pole of the optic vesicle remains static during optic cup formation.
source: As indicated above, the dorsal pole of the optic vesicle remains static (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from imaging data.

claim: The presumptive dorsal CMZ domain either originates from the lens-facing neuroretina or is established secondarily at a later time point.
source: Thus, the presumptive dorsal CMZ domain either originates from the lens-facing neuroretina or, alternatively, is established secondarily at a later time point, like the ventral CMZ in the region of the optic fissure.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation that the dorsal pole remains static.

claim: The identification of lens-averted domains as the source of the future nasal and temporal CMZ is consistent with the hypothesis of a distinct origin of retinal stem cells.
source: The identification of lens-averted domains as the source of the future nasal and temporal CMZ is consistent with the hypothesis of a distinct origin of retinal stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed data to a broader hypothesis.

claim: The entire optic vesicle is initially composed of stem cells that at the lens-facing side respond to a signal to take a progenitor fate.
source: Our data support a scenario in which the entire optic vesicle is initially composed of stem cells that at the lens-facing side respond to a signal to take a progenitor fate.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed patterns of cell behavior and differentiation.

claim: There is a tight coupling of morphogenesis with cell determination by inductive signals derived from the surface ectoderm.
source: We propose a tight coupling of morphogenesis with cell determination by inductive signals derived from the surface ectoderm to explain the successive spreading of retinal differentiation from the center to the periphery (Sinn and Wittbrodt, 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis to explain observed patterns of differentiation.

claim: Lens-averted stem cells might retain their stem cell fate because they are exposed to differentiation signals at the latest point in time.
source: Accordingly, lens-averted stem cells might retain their stem cell fate because they are exposed to that signal at the latest point in time.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the maintenance of stem cell identity.

claim: Stemness might require an active process at the interface to the RPE.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that stemness might require an active process at the interface to the RPE; it is also possible that both scenarios are involved.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: rx2 is initially found in the entire optic vesicle and subsequently is confined to the CMZ.
source: Both scenarios are consistent with the expression pattern of rx2, which is initially found in the entire optic vesicle and subsequently is confined to the CMZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of rx2 expression patterns.

claim: rx2-positive cells of the CMZ represent multipotent retinal stem cells.
source: Strikingly, rx2-positive cells of the CMZ represent multipotent retinal stem cells (Reinhardt, Centanin et al., submitted).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to submitted work.

claim: Cell motility and tissue fluidity are a prerequisite for neuroretinal flow.
source: We demonstrated that cell motility and thus tissue fluidity are a prerequisite for neuroretinal flow.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationship between cell movement and epithelial flow.

claim: BMP has been linked to mobility in other tissues during development.
source: A likely candidate might be BMP, which has been linked to mobility in other tissues during development.
evidence: This is general knowledge about BMP function in development.

claim: In heart jogging, BMP has an 'antimotogenic' effect.
source: In heart jogging, for example, BMP has an 'antimotogenic' effect (Veerkamp et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: BMP signaling is important for the enhancement of RPE and the inhibition of optic cup/neuroretina development.
source: BMP signaling is important for various aspects of vertebrate eye development such as the enhancement of RPE and the inhibition of optic cup/neuroretina development (Fuhrmann et al., 2000; Hyer et al., 2003; Müller et al., 2007; Steinfeld et al., 2013), the formation of the dorso-ventral axis (Behesti et al., 2006; Holly et al., 2014; Koshiba-Takeuchi et al., 2000; Sasagawa et al., 2002), and the induction of the optic fissure (Morcillo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: BMP signaling is important for the formation of the dorso-ventral axis in the eye.
source: BMP signaling is important for various aspects of vertebrate eye development such as the enhancement of RPE and the inhibition of optic cup/neuroretina development (Fuhrmann et al., 2000; Hyer et al., 2003; Müller et al., 2007; Steinfeld et al., 2013), the formation of the dorso-ventral axis (Behesti et al., 2006; Holly et al., 2014; Koshiba-Takeuchi et al., 2000; Sasagawa et al., 2002), and the induction of the optic fissure (Morcillo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: BMP signaling is important for the induction of the optic fissure.
source: BMP signaling is important for various aspects of vertebrate eye development such as the enhancement of RPE and the inhibition of optic cup/neuroretina development (Fuhrmann et al., 2000; Hyer et al., 2003; Müller et al., 2007; Steinfeld et al., 2013), the formation of the dorso-ventral axis (Behesti et al., 2006; Holly et al., 2014; Koshiba-Takeuchi et al., 2000; Sasagawa et al., 2002), and the induction of the optic fissure (Morcillo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Specific regions of the eye depend on the modulation of BMP signaling by the expression of a BMP antagonist.
source: Specific regions of the eye also seem to depend on the modulation of BMP signaling by the expression of a BMP antagonist (Sakuta et al., 2001, French et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BMP signaling is mainly elevated in the temporal domain and to a lesser degree in the nasal domain of the optic vesicle at 16.5 hpf.
source: BMP signaling is mainly elevated in the temporal domain and to a lesser degree in the nasal domain of the optic vesicle (16.5hpf, Figure 4A,B,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pSmad immunohistochemistry and BMP reporter data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At 21.5 hpf BMP signaling is confined to the dorsal pole of the optic cup.
source: At 21.5 hpf BMP signaling is confined to the dorsal pole of the optic cup (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pSmad immunohistochemistry and BMP reporter data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The transcriptional BMP sensor is activated with a delay and shows a more confined area of activity compared to pSmad 1/5/8.
source: The transcriptional BMP sensor is activated with a delay and shows a more confined area of activity (compare Figure 4A–C to Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of pSmad and BMP reporter data in Figure 4.

claim: Fsta is expressed in two domains, a nasal and a temporal domain.
source: Fsta was expressed in two domains, a nasal and a temporal domain (Figure 4G–I and Figure 5A), whereas bambi was only expressed in the temporal domain of the optic vesicle (Figure 4J,K) and the dorsal domain of the optic cup (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Bambi is only expressed in the temporal domain of the optic vesicle and the dorsal domain of the optic cup.
source: Fsta was expressed in two domains, a nasal and a temporal domain (Figure 4G–I and Figure 5A), whereas bambi was only expressed in the temporal domain of the optic vesicle (Figure 4J,K) and the dorsal domain of the optic cup (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The regions of fsta expression correspond to the domains showing neuroretinal flow during optic cup formation.
source: The regions of fsta expression correspond to the domains showing neuroretinal flow during optic cup formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of fsta expression patterns and observed cell movements.

claim: Pan-ocular expression of BMP4 resulted in a strong response of the BMP reporter, indicating pan-ocular BMP4 signaling.
source: The pan-ocular expression of BMP4 resulted in a strong response of the reporter, indicating pan-ocular BMP4 signaling (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by BMP reporter data in experimental embryos shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pan-ocular BMP expression arrested epithelial flow during optic cup formation.
source: Strikingly resembling the BMP dependent 'antimotogenic' effect (Veerkamp et al., 2013), pan-ocular BMP expression arrested epithelial flow during optic cup formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging of BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: Cells in the lens-averted part of the future neuroretina remained in the prospective RPE domain and did not contribute to the optic cup when BMP4 was expressed pan-ocularly.
source: Time-lapse in vivo microscopy revealed that cells in the lens-averted part of the future neuroretina remained in the prospective RPE domain and did not contribute to the optic cup (Video 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data of BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: Pan-ocular BMP expression resulted in an apparently ectopic domain of neuroretina that arose from a morphogenetic failure, rather than from a trans-differentiation of RPE.
source: This ultimately resulted in an apparently ectopic domain of neuroretina that arose from a morphogenetic failure, rather than from a trans-differentiation of RPE (Figure 6D, Fig. 6—figure supplement 1,2,3, Videos 8,9,10).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed phenotype based on time-lapse imaging data.

claim: The severity of the BMP4 overexpression phenotype correlated well with levels of fsta expression in the optic vesicle and was most prominent in the temporal domain.
source: The severity of the phenotype correlated well with levels of fsta expression in the optic vesicle and was most prominent in the temporal domain of the optic vesicle.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of phenotype severity and fsta expression patterns.

claim: The repression of BMP signaling is crucial to mobilize the lens-averted retinal epithelium, causing it to flow and eventually constitute the neural retina to a large extent.
source: We propose that the repression of BMP signaling is crucial to mobilize the lens-averted retinal epithelium, causing it to flow and eventually constitute the neural retina to a large extent.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed effects of BMP manipulation on epithelial flow.

claim: After initiation of neuroretinal differentiation in control embryos, the undifferentiated domains are restricted to the un-fused optic fissure margins and the forming CMZ.
source: After initiation of neuroretinal differentiation in control embryos, the undifferentiated domains are restricted to the un-fused optic fissure margins and the forming CMZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of Rx2 expression in control embryos.

claim: The impairment of neuroretinal flow resulted in a mis-organization of the optic fissure.
source: The impairment of neuroretinal flow, however, resulted in a mis-organization of the optic fissure.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: In BMP4-expressing embryos, the undifferentiated Rx2-expressing domain was found at the ultimate tip of the lens-averted neuroretinal domain, which failed to flow into the optic cup and persisted in the prospective RPE.
source: Here, the undifferentiated Rx2-expressing domain was found at the ultimate tip of the lens-averted neuroretinal domain, which failed to flow into the optic cup and persisted in the prospective RPE (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of Rx2 expression in BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: The temporal optic fissure margin failed to extend into the optic fissure in BMP4-expressing embryos.
source: As a result, the temporal optic fissure margin, in particular, failed to extend into the optic fissure (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data of BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: The nasal optic fissure margin also failed to extend properly into the optic fissure in BMP4-expressing embryos, but to a lesser extent than the temporal margin.
source: This also holds true, but to a lesser extent, to the nasal optic fissure margin (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data of BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: The failure of the two fissure margins to converge results in a persisting optic fissure, a coloboma.
source: As a result, the two fissure margins cannot converge resulting in a persisting optic fissure, a coloboma.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the observed failure of fissure margin extension.

claim: Pan-ocular expression of BMP4 results in phenotypes including a 'Plattauge' (flat-eye), in which the ventral part of the eye is strongly affected.
source: Macroscopically, the pan-ocular expression of BMP4 results in phenotypes including a 'Plattauge' (flat-eye) (Figure 6G), in which the ventral part of the eye is strongly affected and a milder phenotype (Figure 6F), in which the ventral retina develops, but with a persisting optic fissure.
evidence: This claim is supported by macroscopic observations of BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: Pan-ocular expression of BMP4 results in a milder phenotype in which the ventral retina develops, but with a persisting optic fissure.
source: Macroscopically, the pan-ocular expression of BMP4 results in phenotypes including a 'Plattauge' (flat-eye) (Figure 6G), in which the ventral part of the eye is strongly affected and a milder phenotype (Figure 6F), in which the ventral retina develops, but with a persisting optic fissure.
evidence: This claim is supported by macroscopic observations of BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: Exposing the developing eye to high levels of ectopically applied BMP can cause dorsalization, concomitant with a loss of ventral cell identities.
source: It was previously shown that exposing the developing eye to high levels of ectopically applied BMP can cause dorsalization, concomitant with a loss of ventral cell identities (Behesti et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim references previous research findings.

claim: Early BMP4 exposure arrests neuroepithelial flow, resulting in a morphologically affected ventral retina.
source: Our data based on stable BMP4 expression (rx2::BMP4) in the entire optic vesicle, however, conclusively show that early BMP4 exposure arrests neuroepithelial flow, resulting in a morphologically affected ventral retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from stable BMP4 expression experiments.

claim: The ventral expression of vax2 in optic cups of rx2::BMP4 embryos indicates the maintenance of ventral retinal fates and argues against early transdifferentiation/dorsalization induced by BMP.
source: The ventral expression of vax2 in optic cups of rx2::BMP4 embryos indicates the maintenance of ventral retinal fates and argues against early transdifferentiation/dorsalization induced by BMP (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by vax2 expression data in BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: The remaining lens-averted domain in BMP4-expressing embryos, which was ectopically localized and was not integrated into the optic cup, eventually differentiated into neuroretina.
source: Remarkably, the remaining lens-averted domain of those embryos, which was ectopically localized and was not integrated into the optic cup, eventually differentiated into neuroretina (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), as indicated by the expression of vsx1 (Kimura et al., 2008; Shi et al., 2011; Vitorino et al., 2009) and vsx2 (formerly Chx10) (Vitorino et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by marker expression data in BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: A localization of neuroretina within the RPE domain might be mistaken for an RPE to neuroretina trans-differentiation.
source: Notably, a localization of neuroretina within the RPE domain might be mistaken for an RPE to neuroretina trans-differentiation, as proposed for other phenotypes (Araki et al., 2002; Azuma et al., 2005; Sakaguchi et al., 1997, Bankhead et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cautionary note about interpretation of phenotypes, referencing previous literature.

claim: Even in amniotes, the histological analyses of consecutive stages of optic cup development are best interpreted as epithelial flow that also enlarges the retinal surface.
source: Even in amniotes, the histological analyses of consecutive stages of optic cup development are best interpreted as epithelial flow that also enlarges the retinal surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation extending the findings to other vertebrate groups.

claim: Epithelial flow can be appreciated during in vitro optic cup formation using mammalian embryonic stem cells.
source: This can even be appreciated during in vitro optic cup formation using mammalian embryonic stem cells (Eiraku et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on in vitro optic cup formation.

claim: The last cells flowing into the optic cup will eventually constitute the CMZ.
source: Our data have far-reaching implications on the generation of the retinal stem cell niche of teleosts, as the last cells flowing into the optic cup will eventually constitute the CMZ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of epithelial flow and CMZ formation.

claim: A part of the lens-averted epithelium is the primary source of the RPE.
source: We identify a part of the lens-averted epithelium as the primary source of the RPE.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of RPE formation during optic cup development.

claim: The arrest of neuroepithelial flow by the 'antimotogenic' effect of BMP results in coloboma.
source: The arrest of neuroepithelial flow by the 'antimotogenic' effect of BMP (Veerkamp et al., 2013) results in coloboma and thus highlights the importance of the flow through the fissure for the establishment of the ventral optic cup.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing coloboma in BMP4-expressing embryos.

claim: It is unlikely that the bending of the neuroretina provides the motor for the epithelial flow.
source: It is unlikely that the bending of the neuroretina provides the motor for the epithelial flow; in the opo mutant no ectopic neuroretina can be found, indicating that the flow persists, even in the absence of optic cup bending (Bogdanović et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in the opo mutant.

claim: Forces established outside the neuroretina are likely to drive the epithelial flow.
source: Consequently, forces established outside the neuroretina are likely to drive the flow.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the inference that neuroretinal bending is not the driving force.

claim: The mono-layered-forming RPE potentially contributes to the flow by changing its shape from a columnar to a flat epithelium, massively enlarging its surface.
source: One tissue potentially involved is the mono-layered-forming RPE. We speculate that this tissue contributes to the flow by changing its shape from a columnar to a flat epithelium, massively enlarging its surface (Figure 1J–K, Video 3).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism driving epithelial flow.

claim: Epithelial flow is maintained even if cell proliferation is inhibited in both neuroretina and RPE.
source: This remains an interesting point, in particular given that epithelial flow is maintained even if cell proliferation is inhibited in both neuroretina and RPE.
evidence: This claim is supported by aphidicolin treatment experiments.

claim: Aphidicolin efficiently inhibited cell proliferation as shown by drastically reduced pHH3 positive nuclei.
source: Aphidicolin efficiently inhibited cell proliferation shown by drastically reduced pHH3 positive nuclei (upper panel, average of 6 pHH3 positive nuclei) compared to the control (lower panel, average of 21 pHH3 positive nuclei) (the optic cup is encircled with a dotted white line, 21.5 hpf).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of pHH3 positive cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The application of aphidicolin did not affect the epithelial flow.
source: The application of aphidicolin did not affect the epithelial flow.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging of aphidicolin-treated embryos.
